analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited soft money donations to political parties and tightens campaign disclosure and enforcement rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with zero cosponsors, referred to five House committees, and never received a committee markup or floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overhauled how federal campaigns are financed. Its centerpiece was a ban on soft money — the unlimited donations that corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals could give to political parties outside the normal contribution limits. It also would have sped up public disclosure of campaign money on the internet, required faster reporting of last-minute attack ads, barred foreign money and contributions from children, limited members' use of taxpayer-funded mass mailings during election years, stopped fundraising inside federal buildings, banned converting campaign funds to personal use, and roughly doubled penalties for violating campaign finance law. The bill never reached a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would see who is paying for campaign advertising within a day rather than after the election, and candidates who cannot self-fund — the bill offered a voluntary $50,000 cap on spending a candidate's own family wealth in House races. The rules would also have forced parties to run federal election activity through disclosed, limited contributions rather than unlimited ones.

how_it_helps.text: National and state party committees would be barred from soliciting, receiving, or spending soft money — funds not subject to contribution limits and reporting requirements — for federal election activity, and candidates and officeholders could not handle such funds either.

The Federal Election Commission would have to put electronically filed campaign reports on the internet within 24 hours, and last-minute attack ads costing $1,000 or more would have to be reported within 24 hours, so voters could see who paid before Election Day.

It would have banned fundraising on federal property by officials including the President, Vice President, and Members of Congress, and barred members from sending taxpayer-funded mass mailings in the year they run for reelection.

Campaign funds could not be converted to personal use — no mortgage payments, vacations, country club dues, or tuition — and penalties for knowing and willful campaign finance violations would roughly double.

The foreign money ban would be tightened, contributions from minors banned, and tax-exempt organizations would lose their tax exemption if they accepted party or candidate money or ran electioneering ads close to an election.

analysis.who_pays: The main payers would be political party committees that depended on unlimited soft money, large donors who used it, tax-exempt groups doing election-year advertising, labor unions (which would have to rebate nonmember fees spent on politics if asked), and incumbent officeholders facing new limits on franked mail, federal-building fundraising, and personal use of campaign funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Party committees, big donors, unions, incumbents

drawbacks.text: The bill raised some contribution limits at the same time it banned soft money: the aggregate individual contribution limit goes from $25,000 to $30,000, and a new $10,000 annual limit would permit gifts to state party committees, giving the biggest donors somewhat more room in disclosed channels.

It narrows what counts as a regulated 'independent expenditure' to communications that are express advocacy — ads saying 'vote for' or 'defeat' — so issue ads that attack a candidate without explicit advocacy words could escape the reporting rules, a loophole critics of this approach have long pointed to.

The Beck provision requires unions to give nonmember employees an annual objection procedure and rebate the share of their payments spent on politics, which unions opposed as an administrative burden and a cut to their political activity; requiring donor identification at the $50 level also raises privacy concerns for small contributors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine reform package aimed at the soft money system that dominated 1990s campaigns, with faster disclosure and stronger enforcement as its public-facing benefits. Its main cost falls on parties, large donors, unions, and tax-exempt groups rather than on ordinary people, though the modest increase in hard-money limits and the express-advocacy definition are real design weaknesses that would have left some large spending lightly regulated. On balance the costs fall on concentrated interests and the benefits on voters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees, and never scheduled for a committee vote or floor action before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Representative Sander Levin introduced the Campaign Finance Improvement Act of 1998 on March 17, 1998.
No other member cosponsored the bill — its cosponsor list shows zero names.

The same day, the bill was referred to five committees — Oversight, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Government Reform and Oversight, and Judiciary — with jurisdiction 'to be subsequently determined by the Speaker,' a split referral that makes action harder because any committee can sit on it.
In the following weeks it was referred to a Government Management subcommittee (April 1998) and an Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee, and no further action of any kind was taken.
The bill died there when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, having never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The national and state party committees, corporate and union soft-money donors, and incumbents who benefit from the existing rules were better off, because none of the restrictions ever took effect and campaign finance law was left unchanged for that Congress.

for.name: Rep. Sander M. Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pursued no other recorded cosponsors; it was his only action on the measure before it died in committee.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.what_they_did: His committee, the lead referral for election-law bills, never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; no committee action was ever taken.

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: The bill was split across five committees at the Speaker's discretion and he never determined a single committee of jurisdiction or brought the bill to the floor.

against.name: Rep. Dan Burton
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Government Reform and Oversight
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral and never acted on the bill.

against.name: House leadership and committee chairs, 105th Congress
against.role: The five committees and Speaker holding the referral
against.what_they_did: No committee ever reported the bill, and the House never voted on it at any point in 1998.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever held, so no partisan breakdown exists; it simply died in committee.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill bans party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending soft money — unlimited donations outside federal limits — for federal election activity, and bars party committees from channeling money to tax-exempt groups. Parties would have had to run federal campaigns entirely through disclosed, limited contributions. The bill does modestly raise some hard-money limits as a trade.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and wealthy contributors
industries.note: Coordination rules would treat anything of value provided in coordination with a candidate as a capped contribution, foreign money and children's contributions would be banned, and donor identification would be required at $50. Donors using undisclosed channels to influence elections would have lost the ability to do so anonymously or outside limits.

Groups exempt under 501(c)(3) or (c)(4) would lose their tax exemption if they took or gave party or candidate money or ran 'electioneering advertising' within 60 days of a general election. This targeted the practice of routing political money through nonprofits.

The bill codifies the Beck decision: unions would have to notify nonmember fee-payers annually and rebate the share of their payments spent on politics, cutting into union political funds. Unions also lose the ability to give soft money to party committees like any other donor.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and federal officeholders
industries.note: Incumbents would face new limits: no taxpayer-funded mass mailings in election years, no fundraising inside federal buildings (with penalties up to three years' imprisonment), a ban on converting campaign funds to personal use, and doubled penalties for violations. These provisions constrain the officeholders who would have had to vote on the bill.
